terminal.description: A shell that starts in the shop's top folder. Run each script after every change and read what it prints.

tasks.title: Save the evening commands in a script
tasks.description:
Make `evening.sh` in the top folder with Idris's four evening commands from `today.txt`, one per line, in that order. `sh evening.sh` then runs all four.

Check gives a copy of the top folder an `orders/today.csv` of its own, runs `sh evening.sh` there, and compares what it prints with what Idris's commands print.
nextSteps: Run Idris's four commands one at a time and read what each prints.
Make an empty `evening.sh` with `touch` and open it from the file panel.
Write the four commands in it, one per line, exactly as `today.txt` has them.
Run `sh evening.sh` and compare with what you saw.
hints: A script holds the commands you would type, one per line.
The file needs nothing but Idris's four lines. `sh evening.sh` runs them in the folder you are in.
Write these four lines in evening.sh: `echo "Orders today:"`, `wc -l < orders/today.csv`, `echo "Unpaid:"` and `grep -c unpaid orders/today.csv`.

docs.title: sh: the shell that runs scripts

tasks.title: Make evening.sh a program
tasks.description:
Give `evening.sh` a first line that names `sh` (or `bash`), and let its owner run it, so that `./evening.sh` works from the top folder.

Check reads the first line of `evening.sh` and its permissions, then runs `./evening.sh` in a copy of the top folder and compares what it prints with what Idris's commands print.
nextSteps: Run `./evening.sh` now and read the message.
Add the first line from the lesson at the very top of the file.
Give the owner `x` with `chmod`, then run `ls -l evening.sh`.
hints: Two things are missing: the line that names the program, and the permission to run.
The first line starts with `#!`, followed by the full path of `sh`. `chmod u+x` lets the owner run the file.
Make `#!/bin/sh` the first line of evening.sh, then run `chmod u+x evening.sh`.

tasks.title: Count the file it is given
tasks.description:
Change `count.sh` so that it prints how many orders, that is lines, are in the file named by its first argument, as in `./count.sh orders/2026-04-02.csv`. It must work from any folder, with the path given from that folder, and with a file name that has a space in it.

Check runs `count.sh` with `sh` on files of its own: once from the top folder, and once from inside another folder, on a name with a space. Each time, a line of what it prints must start with the right number.
nextSteps: Run `sh count.sh orders/2026-04-02.csv` and see that it counts another file.
Find the line that names `orders/today.csv`, and put the first argument there instead.
Try it on each file in `orders`, and compare with `wc -l`.
hints: Sol's script names one file by hand. The lesson's part on arguments shows how a script gets the file you give it.
`$1` is the first argument. Keep it in double quotes, and put no folder in front of it.

tasks.title: Say when it fails
tasks.description:
When `count.sh` counted, it prints the number, then `Counted.`, and ends with exit status 0. When the file does not exist, it must not print `Counted.`, and its exit status must not be 0.

Check runs `count.sh` with `sh` on a file of its own and on a file that does not exist, and reads what it prints and its exit status each time.
nextSteps: Run `sh count.sh nowhere.csv`, then `echo $?`, and read both.
Find which line decides the status the script ends with.
Make `Counted.` print only when the count worked.
Run both cases again, with `echo $?` after each.
hints: A script ends with the status of its last command, and here that is the `echo`.
`&&` runs the next command only if the one before it worked, and the line keeps the failed status when it did not.
Make the two lines one: `wc -l < "$1" && echo "Counted."`.
